issues.note: Overlaps d2-006 heavily. d2-006 front: 'A tool description should answer four questions about the tool. What are they?' d2-009 back returns three of those same four items ('accepted input formats with examples, when to choose this tool over the neighbouring one, and when not to use it at all'). Corpus source is one bullet list: 'What it does / What input it accepts (formats, ID types, examples) / When to use it vs similar tools / When NOT to use it (boundary cases)' (Domain-2_v2 §2.2). Keep only if the front is re-cut to drill the diagnostic move rather than re-listing the bullets.

suggested.text: Both tool descriptions already say what their tool does and the model still confuses them. Which single description element most directly separates the two?

issues.note: The front names the answer. 'Token binding beats a server-side timing heuristic, an orchestration-layer confirmation prompt, and a prompt instruction. What does it have that none of them do?' — the winner is handed over, so only the adjective is being recalled. CARD-SPEC §10: 'Do not put the answer in the front.'

suggested.text: A server-side timing heuristic, an orchestration-layer confirmation prompt, and a prompt instruction all try to force a preview before a destructive call. What does the two-tool design provide that none of the three does?

issues.note: Back says 'Resources for stable data the agent needs to read'. The corpus never characterises resource data as stable, and the word inverts the contrast it draws: 'resources are requested on demand; a static dump bloats context and goes stale' (Domain-2_v2 §2.6). Freshness-on-demand is the resource's advantage over a pasted dump; teaching 'stable' risks Ram picking the system-prompt-dump distractor for changing data.

suggested.text: Resources for data the agent needs to read — catalogs, schemas, documentation hierarchies, fetched on demand. Tools for actions the agent needs to take.

issues.note: Same question as d2-037 in different words. d2-037 front: 'Which MCP config file does a team commit to the repository, and which one stays on the individual developer's machine?' d2-059 front: 'Which MCP configuration file travels with the repository, and which one stays on a single machine?' Both backs give `.mcp.json` project root / `~/.claude.json` user home. CARD-SPEC §10: 'Do not write two cards that ask the same thing in different words.' d2-037 is the keeper (it carries the `known-gap`/`d2.2` tags).

Typed `trap` but the `trap` field states no misconception a candidate holds — 'both files configure MCP servers identically, so the deciding line is sharing scope rather than capability' is a restatement of the back.

Duplicates d2-038. d2-038 back: 'Into `.mcp.json` with `${GITHUB_TOKEN}` substitution and the variable documented in the README — Claude Code expands it from the environment at runtime.' d2-060 back: 'Claude Code substitutes the value from the environment at runtime, so the config can be committed while the credential stays out of the repo.' Same fact, same trap pair (user-scope split vs committed placeholder token). d2-038 is the richer card and is the keeper.

Cite order wrong if kept. Primary is `Key-Distinctions_v1 #2`, which only says '→ `.mcp.json` with `${GITHUB_TOKEN}` env var substitution.' The claim being drilled — runtime expansion from the environment — lives in Domain-2_v2 §2.6: 'At runtime, Claude Code substitutes the variable from the environment. This lets project config be version-controlled while credentials stay out of the repo.' Domain-2_v2 §2.6 must come first.

Primary cite does not hold the claim. `Key-Distinctions_v1 #9` splits errors only two ways — 'Transient (timeout, network)' vs 'Permanent (syntax error, not found)' — and never names validation, permission, or business. The back's three-way permanent breakdown comes from Domain-2_v2 §2.3: 'The exam distinguishes four categories of tool error' with the Transient / Validation / Business / Permission table. CARD-SPEC §6: 'The primary cite comes first, and it must be the section the back's claim is actually drawn from.'

Overlaps d2-013 ('Of the four error categories, which one should the agent retry unchanged?' / 'Transient only'). Retain only if the front is kept on the retry/no-retry split across all four rather than re-asking which one retries.

Covers the same ground as d2-016 ('A `search_orders` query runs fine and matches nothing. What should the tool return?') plus d2-017 (masked access failure). Its two-part front is a slightly distinct angle, so it is salvageable, but with d2-016 and d2-017 already in the deck this is the third pass over Domain-2_v2 §2.3 'Valid Empty Results vs Access Failures'. Cut one of the three.

Same question as d2-005. d2-005 front: 'An agent picks the wrong one of two similar tools about half the time. What do you inspect before adding any new component to the system?' d2-063 front: 'Two similarly named tools are misrouted 45% of the time. What do you repair before adding anything new?' Identical answer (the descriptions) and an identical pre-routing-classifier trap. It also overlaps d2-007, which already carries the 45% figure and the `extract_web_results` rename.

Invents a parameter. The front asks about 'merging two confusable tools into a single tool with a mode parameter'; the corpus records the consolidation anti-pattern with no such parameter — 'Combine into single `lookup_entity` tool (loses semantic precision)' (Domain-2_v2 §2.2). CARD-SPEC §10 forbids inventing parameters. Use the corpus's own shape.

suggested.text: Why is merging two confusable tools into a single `lookup_entity` tool the wrong repair?

issues.note: The same consolidation trap is already the `trap` field of d2-008: 'merging them into one `lookup_entity` tool ends the confusion by discarding the semantic precision that made two tools worth having.'

Same question as d2-022. d2-022 front: 'Why does a `dry_run: boolean` parameter fail as a mandatory-preview mechanism?' d2-065 front: 'Why can a `dry_run` boolean parameter never guarantee that a preview happened?' Both backs say the agent can call with `dry_run` false directly. d2-022 is the keeper.

Same question as d2-021. d2-021 front: 'A removal operation must always be previewed before it executes. What tool design makes skipping the preview impossible?' d2-066 front: 'What tool shape makes a mandatory preview architecturally impossible to skip?' Both backs describe the preview call returning a single-use confirmation token that the execute call requires. d2-021 is the keeper (it names `preview_remove_member` / `execute_remove_member` as the corpus does).

Same question as d2-045. d2-045 front: 'Bulk deletions affecting more than 50 records must always be escalated. Why does the exam pick a `PreToolUse` hook over a system-prompt rule?' d2-067 front: 'A bulk deletion touching more than 50 records must always route to human approval. What enforces that?' Both backs land on the `PreToolUse` hook and the deterministic-vs-probabilistic contrast from Domain-2_v2 §2.7. If either survives, prefer d2-067's `trap` line ('`PostToolUse` fires after execution, so it logs the breach it was supposed to prevent') grafted onto d2-045, since that is the only content here d2-045 lacks.

Same content as d2-032. d2-032 front: 'What are MCP's three primitives, and what does each one provide?' d2-068 back also enumerates all three ('Tools are actions Claude calls. Resources are read-only data Claude reads. Prompts are the third primitive: reusable templates'), so the narrower front is answered by re-reciting d2-032's card. d2-032 is the keeper.

Same question as d2-033. d2-033 front: 'An agent burns turn after turn calling `search_issues` with guessed queries just to discover what issues exist. Which MCP primitive removes that?' d2-069 front: 'An agent burns turns guessing search queries just to discover what records exist in a project tracker. What do you expose to it?' Both backs: expose a summary catalog as an MCP resource, then make targeted tool calls. Its system-prompt-dump trap already exists as d2-035.

Collapses d2-040 and d2-041 into one card without adding anything. d2-040 already gives the root cause ('The MCP tool's description does not make its advantage explicit, and tool selection runs on descriptions') and d2-041 already gives the disable-Grep trap. All three trace to the same Domain-2_v2 §2.6 'MCP Tool Descriptions vs Built-in Tools' block.

Tagged `known-gap` + `d2.1` while d2-040 and d2-041, which carry the same content, are untagged. Whichever card survives, the gap tagging must be consistent — `d2.1` is 'Tool description design', so it belongs on all three or none.

Same question as d2-030. d2-030 back: 'Set `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"}` on the first request, then relax to `"auto"` for the following turns.' d2-071 back is the same instruction with the same trap ('leaving the forced value on every turn means the enrichment tools can never be called at all'). d2-030 is the keeper — its front carries the corpus's own ~90% prompt-compliance detail (Domain-2_v2 §2.5).

Wrong known-gap tag. Tagged `known-gap` + `d4.5`, but CARD-SPEC §7 defines `d4.5` as '`stop_reason` / `tool_use` API mechanics'. This card is about `tool_choice` forcing and sequencing — it touches neither `stop_reason` nor the `tool_use` block, so it inflates the d4.5 gap count with unrelated material.

Fabricated premise. The front asserts '`{"type": "any"}` keeps letting other tools go first' as the situation being fixed. Domain-2_v2 §2.5's forced-first-step scenario has no such step — its rejected options are 'Strengthen the prompt instruction' and 'Leave `tool_choice` forced on every turn'. The behaviour claimed is not false, but it is not in the corpus and should not be drilled as if it were.

Same question as d2-049. d2-049 front: 'You need every file that references a deprecated `formatDate` function. Which built-in tool finds them?' d2-072 front: 'You need every file that calls a deprecated `formatDate` function. Grep or Glob?' Both backs are Grep with the identical `**/formatDate*` Glob trap from Domain-2_v2 §2.9. d2-049 is the keeper; d2-072's front is additionally weaker because 'Grep or Glob?' reduces it to a coin flip.

Same question as d2-053. d2-053 front: 'After an Edit fails on a non-unique anchor, a teammate retries with a shorter, more generic anchor string. What happens?' d2-073 front: 'Why does retrying a failed Edit with a shorter anchor string make the problem worse?' Both backs say a shorter string is likelier to be non-unique (Domain-2_v2 §2.9: 'shorter anchors are *more* likely to be non-unique, not less'). The Read + Write fallback is already d2-052 and the `sed` trap is already d2-054, so this card adds nothing.
